The President makes these appointments after consulting with the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, the Governor of the state, and the Chief Justice of the High Court. The number of judges in a High Court varies by state, with smaller states having fewer judges than larger states. Additional judges can be appointed to clear pending cases, but their tenure is limited to two years. No one over the age of 62 can be appointed as a High Court judge.

subtopic: Judiciary — Supreme Court and High Courts
stem: The power to extend or restrict the jurisdiction of the High Court rests with :
solution: The power to extend or restrict the jurisdiction of the High Court rests with the Parliament. Article 230 of the Indian Constitution gives Parliament the power to extend or exclude the jurisdiction of a High Court to or from any Union territory. It also states that the State Legislature cannot increase, restrict, or abolish the jurisdiction of a High Court. The High Court has original jurisdiction, which is the power to hear cases for the first time. Some examples of cases that fall under the High Court’s original jurisdiction include cases related to revenue, admiralty, contempt of court, probate, and marriages.

solution: A Money Bill can be introduced in the state legislature on the recommendation of the Governor. A Money Bill shall be introduced only in a Legislative Assembly, not in Legislative council. Money Bill refers to a bill (draft law) introduced in the lower Chamber of Indian Parliament (Lok Sabha) which generally covers the issue of receipt and spending of money, such as tax laws, laws governing borrowing, and expenditure of the government, prevention of black money. Money bills passed by the Lok Sabha are sent to the Rajya Sabha (the upper house of parliament, elected by the state and territorial legislatures or appointed by the president). subject: Polity

stem: The members of the State Legislative Assembly participate in the election of:
solution: Take the three bodies named in turn. For the President, Article 54 lays down an electoral college made up of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament together with the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, so a member of a State Legislative Assembly is part of that college. For the Vice-President, Article 66 confines the electoral college to the members of both Houses of Parliament alone, so a State Assembly member has no vote there. For the Legislative Council of a State, Article 171 divides the House among several constituencies, and one-third of its members are elected by the members of the Legislative Assembly of that State. The Assembly member therefore takes part in two of the three elections named - that of the President and that of one-third of the Legislative Council - and in neither case in the election of the Vice-President. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED A -> D. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints A. Basis: Three constitutional provisions settle this. Article 54: the electoral college for the President consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament AND the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (Article 54 read with the 70th Amendment extends it to Delhi and Puducherry). So MLAs do vote for the President. Article 66: the Vice-President is elected by the members of both Houses of Parliament only - MLAs have no part, which is the standard trap in this stem. Article 171(3)(d): one-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by the members of the Legislative Assembly. So MLAs vote there too. President plus Legislative Council members, not the Vice-President.]

stem: Members of the State legislature can focus the attention of the government on matters of public importance through:
solution: 1. Adjournment Motion: It is a parliamentary procedure that allows a member of the legislature to interrupt the normal business of the house to raise a matter of urgent public importance. The member who moves the motion must state the reasons for its urgency and seek the house’s permission to discuss the issue immediately. If the house agrees, the normal business of the house is adjourned, and the issue raised in the motion is discussed. 2. No-confidence Motion: It is a parliamentary procedure that is used to test the government’s strength in the legislature. If a motion of no- confidence is passed against the government, it must resign from office. 3. Censure Motion: It is a parliamentary procedure that is used to express the legislature’s disapproval of the government’s actions or policies. The motion does not have any legal consequences, but it puts pressure on the government to correct its policies. 4. Cut Motion: It is a parliamentary procedure that is used to reduce the amount of money allocated for a particular government program. The member who moves the cut motion must state the reasons for its necessity and seek the house’s permission to reduce the allocated amount.

All of these methods are available to the Chief Minister to get rid of a minister.

stem: A rift valley is formed mainly due to:
optA: forces of tension in the earth’s crust.
optB: the subsidence of the floor of a river valley.
optC: the valley formed after the formation of fold mountains.
optD: the deepening of a valley by ice action.
solution: The landform in question is not simply a low strip of ground - it is a block of the crust that has sunk between two roughly parallel faults, leaving steep fault scarps facing each other across a flat floor. Faults of that kind, in which one side slips downward along the fault plane, form where the crust is being stretched, so the cause is a pulling apart of the crust rather than a squeezing of it. The great rift systems bear this out: the East African Rift and the Rhine valley both lie where the crust is under extension. The other explanations describe different landforms. The subsidence of a river valley floor produces no matching pair of fault scarps. Fold mountains are built by compression, and the low ground between two folds is a syncline, not a rift. Finally, a valley deepened by moving ice is broadened into the familiar U-shaped glacial trough. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED B -> A. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints B. Basis: A rift valley, or graben, is a block of crust that has dropped down between two roughly parallel normal faults. Normal faulting is the signature of extension: the crust is pulled apart, the hanging wall slides down the fault plane, and the floor subsides. This is what produces the East African Rift, the Rhine graben and the Narmada-Tapi troughs. The distractors describe other landforms: a river valley floor subsiding gives no parallel fault scarps; the low ground between fold mountains is a synclinal valley formed under compression; a valley deepened by ice is a U-shaped glacial trough. Note the older 'ramp valley' idea that a graben can be produced by compression squeezing the flanking blocks upward exists, but the mainstream and exam answer for the main cause of a rift valley is tension.]

stem: The water table is very low in a region where:
optB: runoff water is greater due to torrential rain.
optC: the area is arid with little vegetation.
solution: Water table, also called groundwater table, upper level of an underground surface in which the soil or rocks are permanently saturated with water. The water table fluctuates both with the seasons and from year to year because it is affected by climatic variations and by the amount of precipitation used by vegetation. It also is affected by withdrawing excessive amounts of water from wells or by recharging them artificially. The groundwater may be from precipitation or from groundwater flowing into the aquifer. In areas with sufficient precipitation, water infiltrates through pore spaces in the soil, passing through the unsaturated zone. At increasing depths, water fills in more of the pore spaces in the soils, until a zone of saturation is reached.

solution: The length of coast is what identifies the territory. Lakshadweep, though entirely a group of islands, has a coastline of about 132 kilometres, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands run to roughly nineteen hundred kilometres, so both are far too long. The second detail confirms it: Puducherry keeps a substantial agricultural sector, growing paddy, sugarcane and pulses on its irrigated plains, so a large share of its people live by farming even alongside its marine fishing villages. Matches option B.

2. Satara was the first state to be annexed under the policy of Doctrine of Lapse.
Select the correct answers using the codes given below
solution: Take the two statements separately. The Doctrine of Lapse was the annexation policy pressed by Lord Dalhousie in the years after 1848. Under it, a princely state dependent on the Company whose ruler died leaving no male heir was held to have lapsed, and passed into Company territory; the customary right of a childless ruler to adopt a successor was refused recognition, which is what gave the policy its bite. The first statement therefore describes the rule correctly. Turning to the second, the earliest annexation carried out on this ground was that of Satara in 1848, on the death of its raja without a son of his own. The annexations of Jaitpur and Sambalpur followed in 1849, Udaipur in 1852, and Jhansi and Nagpur in 1854, so Satara does stand first in the sequence. Both statements are thus accurate. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED B -> C. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints B. Basis: Statement 1 is the textbook definition of Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse: a dependent princely state whose ruler died without a male heir would lapse to the Company, the ruler's right to adopt a successor being disallowed. Statement 2 is also correct - Satara was annexed in 1848 and is universally given as the first state taken under the doctrine, with Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1854) and Nagpur (1854) following. So both hold and the answer is 'both'. One pedantic caveat, recorded because it is the likeliest source of a rival derivation: the doctrine's trigger was strictly the absence of a NATURAL male heir, since it annexed states even where a lawfully adopted son existed, so the phrase 'legal male heir' in statement 1 is loose. A second, weaker caveat is that the doctrine applied to dependent states rather than to 'any' princely state. Neither looseness rises to a factual reversal at this level, and both NCERT and standard prep material state the rule in exactly the words used here, so statement 1 reads as correct. Confidence is medium on account of that first caveat.]

Flotation means the weight of the displaced liquid balances the weight of the instrument, so \(\rho V g = m g\). The acceleration due to gravity appears on both sides of that equation and cancels, leaving \(V = m/\rho\). The depth to which the stem sinks is therefore fixed by the density of the liquid alone, with no dependence whatever on the local strength of gravity. The same conclusion follows from the definition of the quantity being measured: specific gravity is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water, a pure number with no reference to gravity in it at all. On a mountain top gravity is indeed slightly weaker, but it weakens the upthrust and the instrument's own weight by precisely the same factor, so the instrument comes to rest at the very same mark on its scale. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED C -> D. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints C. Independently, specific gravity is defined as a ratio of two densities and is dimensionless, so it cannot depend on g even in principle. At altitude g is a little smaller, but it reduces the buoyant force and the instrument's weight in exactly the same proportion, so the reading is unchanged. The tempting wrong answer is 'less', from noticing that buoyancy falls with g while forgetting that the weight it balances falls by the identical factor.]

At A = 60: (60 - 15)/60 = 45/60 = 0.75, so B = 25 + 0.75 x 100 = 100 deg. Endpoint sanity check passes: A = 15 maps to B = 25 and A = 75 maps to B = 125. stem: A ray of light falls on a transparent glass plate. A part of it is reflected and a part is refracted. The reflected and refracted rays can be perpendicular to each other for:
optB: angle of incidence equal to zero
optD: more than one angle of incidence
solution: Let the angle of incidence be \(i\) and the angle of refraction be \(r\), both measured from the normal. The reflected ray leaves at \(i\) on the far side of the normal from the incident ray, while the refracted ray continues into the glass at \(r\) on the other side of the surface, so the angle contained between the reflected and refracted rays is \(180^{\circ} - i - r\). Requiring the two to be perpendicular gives \(180^{\circ} - i - r = 90^{\circ}\), that is \(i + r = 90^{\circ}\), so \(r = 90^{\circ} - i\). Substituting this into Snell's law \(\sin i = n \sin r\) gives \(\sin i = n \sin(90^{\circ} - i) = n \cos i\), and dividing through by \(\cos i\) leaves \(\tan i = n\). For a particular glass plate the refractive index \(n\) is one fixed number, and the tangent increases steadily from zero as the angle runs from \(0^{\circ}\) towards \(90^{\circ}\), so the equation \(\tan i = n\) is satisfied at exactly one angle - about \(56^{\circ}\) for ordinary glass of index \(1.5\). This is the polarising angle. The extremes fail: at normal incidence the reflected and refracted rays travel in opposite directions along the same normal, an angle of \(180^{\circ}\), and at grazing incidence the light is not transmitted into the plate at all. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED D -> C. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints D. Basis: Let i be the angle of incidence and r the angle of refraction. The reflected ray leaves at i on the other side of the normal, so the angle between the reflected and refracted rays is 180 - i - r. Setting that equal to 90 gives i + r = 90, so r = 90 - i. Snell's law sin i = n sin r then becomes sin i = n cos i, i.e. tan i = n. For a given plate n is a single fixed number, so tan i = n has exactly one solution in the range 0 to 90 - the Brewster or polarising angle (56.3 degrees for n = 1.5, verified numerically: sin(56.31) = 0.83205 = 1.5*sin(33.69), and 180 - 56.31 - 33.69 = 90.00). Hence one angle only. Zero incidence sends the reflected and refracted rays back along the same normal in opposite directions, 180 degrees apart, not 90; at 90 degrees the light grazes and nothing enters the plate.]

subject: Biology
stem: Which part of brain controls fine movement, maintains balance and equilibrium of the body and muscle tone in a human being?
solution: The cerebellum is the part of the brain that controls fine movement, maintains balance and equilibrium, and muscle tone. The cerebellum is responsible for coordinating movement, maintaining balance and posture, and muscle tone. It also plays a role in motor learning and cognitive functions like attention and language. The cerebellum is located at the back of the brain, tucked underneath the cerebral hemispheres. It’s often called the “little brain” because it looks like a smaller version of the cerebrum. The cerebellum receives input from the spinal cord and other parts of the brain, and integrates this information to fine-tune motor activity. Damage to the cerebellum can cause disorders in fine movement, equilibrium, posture, and motor learning.
